sections.body: The source defines shadercoding through the shader itself: a GPU-directed program involved in the rendering pipeline. Its taxonomy of vertex, tessellation, geometry, and fragment shaders gives readers a concrete account of where code enters image production. This matters because the later art argument depends on treating code as the actual medium of visual formation, not as a hidden support tool.
sections.heading: Technical Object Of Study

sections.body: The authors emphasize fragment shaders because they convert pixel positions into colors and can use formulas, time variables, and external inputs to generate animated images. That framing makes shadercoding legible as a generative practice: the image is computed from mathematical relations, and interaction can be incorporated into the same visual procedure.
sections.heading: Fragment Shaders As Generators

sections.body: Raymarching is presented as the technique that lets fragment shaders recover 3D depth. The source explains the procedure in terms of distance functions, rays launched per pixel, stepwise traversal, and encounters with objects described by signed distance fields. This supports the claim that mathematical scene descriptions can produce complex real-time visual spaces.
sections.heading: Raymarching And Spatial Depth

sections.body: The article repeatedly rejects a simple opposition between technical constraint and creative expression. Mathematical fluency, spatial reasoning, vector operations, and shader language mastery are treated as conditions of artistic agency. In this account, the artist gains expressive freedom not by avoiding technical systems, but by understanding them deeply enough to improvise inside them.
sections.heading: Technique As Artistic Condition

sections.body: Shader Showdowns supply the article's clearest institutional performance frame: a public, timed event where participants code a shader effect in roughly half an hour and are judged on image, code technique, and visual evolution. The visibility of writing code makes the procedure itself part of the artwork's reception, alongside the generated image.
sections.heading: Live Coding As Performance Frame

sections.body: The source is strongest as conceptual and practice-based analysis. Its evidence includes technical definitions, procedural descriptions, cited aesthetic theory, event formats, and first-person accounts from Revision 2016 and 2018. It does not provide quantitative audience data or comparative studies, so broad claims about digital-art performance should be read as argued interpretation rather than measured generalization.
sections.heading: Evidence And Limits

source_dossier.summary_long: Florine Fouquart and Chu-Yin Chen present shadercoding as a practice located at the junction of GPU programming, mathematics, computer graphics, and performance art. The article begins with a technical introduction: shaders are GPU programs that participate in rendering, fragment shaders map pixel positions to colors, and mathematical formulas can generate patterns, animation, and interactivity. Raymarching receives particular attention because it lets a fragment shader recover three-dimensional depth by casting rays through distance-field descriptions of space, making complex forms and repeated spaces available in real time. This technical exposition is not an end in itself. The authors use it to question the figure of the digital artist as a technical artist whose aesthetic choices are formed through scientific and mathematical processes. The article then shifts into a practice-based reflection on live coding, especially Shader Showdown events where participants write visual shader effects in 25 or 30 minutes before an audience. The source argues that constraint, visibility, and time pressure can become generative. Rather than separating technique from expression, the authorial account describes technical mastery as the condition that allows improvisation, bodily absorption, and dialogue with spectators. The strongest evidence is explanatory and experiential: a shader pipeline taxonomy, descriptions of fragment-shader and raymarching procedures, a concrete vector-math lighting example, the judging structure of Shader Showdowns, and a first-person account of reaching the Revision 2018 final. The result is a source best read as theoretical-practical commentary rather than empirical validation. It establishes a vocabulary for understanding shadercoding as art, but its general claims about performance rest on reflective experience, cited aesthetic theory, and examples from live-coding culture rather than systematic audience or practitioner study.
source_dossier.summary_short: Fouquart and Chen frame shadercoding as both GPU graphics technique and live digital-art practice. They explain fragment shaders, raymarching, distance fields, and mathematical image generation, then connect those techniques to Shader Showdown performance. The source argues that technical mastery and constraint can enable expressive real-time improvisation.

sections.body: The source frames crowd rendering as the intersection of two expensive tasks: navigating a polygon-heavy city and animating many human agents. Its key proposition is that distant avatars do not need full polygonal treatment when image-based impostors can preserve plausible appearance at interactive rates. This motivates the entire pipeline rather than treating texture compression or recoloring as isolated optimizations.
sections.heading: Rendering Problem

sections.body: The most specific rendering-quality argument concerns popping when the viewpoint changes. A conventional plane perpendicular to the sampling camera ignores object shape, while the full PCA best-fit plane can introduce distortions. The compromise is to perturb the conventional plane toward the PCA-derived orientation, reducing visible popping for human impostors while keeping artifacts bounded.
sections.heading: Impostor Plane Choice

sections.body: The memory strategy has two layers. First, symmetric walking motion reduces directional samples, and rectangle packing removes unused texture space around each prerendered human. Second, OpenGL compression provides a further 1:4 reduction and preserves alpha values, making a multi-type, multi-frame human library plausible within the cited 25 Mbyte budget.
sections.heading: Texture Memory Strategy

sections.body: Visual variety comes from recoloring regions rather than generating a fully distinct model for every person. Alpha-channel masks identify body regions such as clothes, hair, and skin; multipass rendering then modulates selected regions with different colors. The source is careful to note a trade-off: additional passes and regions can improve variety but may reduce rendering speed.
sections.heading: Avatar Variety Mechanism

sections.body: The renderer is paired with simple environmental state. Regular floor tiles encode collision and shadow information, giving agents local movement decisions and preventing occupied-destination conflicts. The impostor database is also reused to project human shadows, which adds environmental visual integration at only one extra polygon per avatar shadow.
sections.heading: Behavior and Shadows

sections.body: The reported results support the system-level claim but should be read with their constraints. On an 800-MHz Pentium III with a GeForce GTS2, the system displays 10,000 humans in a 41,260-polygon village at 12 to 20 frames per second. The frame-rate series also shows that the static city already costs much of the budget and that crowd scaling is close to linear in time per frame.
sections.heading: Benchmark Interpretation

sections.body: The method assumes viewers remain far enough from avatars for orthographic impostors and limited texture dimensions to hold up. It also assumes effectively sun-like lighting for shadow reuse and relies on synthetic models rather than captured humans. The authors identify hybrid polygonal close-ups, normal-map shading, culling, photographic acquisition, and richer behavior as future improvements.
sections.heading: Assumptions and Limits

source_dossier.summary_long: The article addresses a specific graphics bottleneck: populated virtual cities require both large static environments and many animated human agents, but fully polygonal crowds make real-time display expensive. Tecchia, Loscos, and Chrysanthou therefore use image-based impostors for distant humans, exploiting the typical viewing conditions of urban walkthroughs where many people are visible but not necessarily close to the camera. Their approach is not just a generic billboard substitution. They tune the impostor representation for walking human geometry, reduce the texture-memory footprint of prerendered samples, and use multipass rendering to create visual variety from a limited set of human models. The technical path is pragmatic: reduce the number of polygons per person, retain enough directional and animation sampling to avoid severe artifacts, and spend saved memory on more types and appearances. Several pieces of evidence anchor the proposal. A PCA-informed plane-selection argument explains how the system reduces viewpoint-change popping without fully adopting a distortion-prone best-fitting plane. Packing each sample into its smallest rectangle cuts memory to 25 percent of the original sample layout, and OpenGL texture compression further reduces frame storage while retaining alpha data for later recoloring. Alpha-channel masks then support multipass rendering, changing clothes and other body regions while preserving the baked shading in the source texture. The implementation also integrates a grid for collision and shadowing, and reuses impostor silhouettes to create posture-aware shadows with one additional polygon. The benchmark demonstrates the intended scale: six avatar types, 10,000 different humans, a 41,260-polygon village, and measured frame rates that remain interactive despite falling as crowd size grows. The source is strongest as a systems paper showing how several approximate techniques combine into a usable real-time renderer; its limits are equally clear, including assumptions about camera distance, sunlight-like illumination, synthetic source models, and the need for culling and richer behavior in future work.
source_dossier.summary_short: This source presents an image-based rendering pipeline for animated crowds in virtual cities. It combines optimized impostors, texture packing, compression, alpha-guided recoloring, and grid-based behavior support. The implementation reports 10,000 varied humans in a 41,260-polygon village at interactive frame rates.

sections.body: The paper argues that the skeleton of an inflated edge-cluster shape is a natural bundling guide because skeletons are locally centered within elongated shapes. Once similar edges are clustered, their surrounding distance-field shape captures a shared corridor, and its skeleton provides the central path along which those edges can be drawn.
sections.heading: Core Argument

sections.body: The first technical step compares uniformly sampled edge trajectories and uses hierarchical agglomerative clustering to find spatially close, same-direction edge groups. Each cluster drawing is then inflated by a distance threshold into a compact shape, making skeletonization possible even though the original input consists of graph edges rather than filled regions.
sections.heading: Clustering And Shape Construction

sections.body: The attraction formula moves sampled edge points toward skeleton feature-transform locations, with an arc-length weighting that leaves endpoints fixed and moves middle points most strongly. This is essential for graph drawings because nodes must remain at their original positions while edges bend into shared bundles.
sections.heading: Attraction Mechanics

sections.body: A direct feature-transform advection field can create sharp kinks near discontinuities. The paper addresses this by assigning each edge to a skeleton path through its endpoint feature points and remapping special off-path attraction cases onto that path, making the attraction smoother and more stable.
sections.heading: Robustness Measures

sections.body: SBEB is not a one-shot operation: it reclusters repeatedly as edges move closer together. A high initial similarity threshold creates reliable fine-scale bundles, then decreasing thresholds allow those already coherent bundles to merge into larger structures without immediately grouping unrelated crossing edges.
sections.heading: Progressive Bundling

sections.body: The implementation treats shapes, skeletons, distance transforms, and attraction largely as image-space operations. Reported table measurements show millisecond-scale CUDA primitives and total GPU times of a few to tens of seconds across tested datasets, supporting the claim that hardware acceleration is central to the method's practicality.
sections.heading: Implementation And Performance

sections.body: The paper gives users postprocessing controls over smoothing, relaxation, and cushion shading. These controls matter because skeleton-guided layouts can look sharply organic or smoother and more force-directed-like, and shaded profiles help users follow overlapping bundles without changing the computed screen-space thickness.
sections.heading: Visual Control

sections.body: The authors explicitly caution that bundling destroys information by overdraw, loss of individual-edge identity, and direction distortion. The method should therefore be interpreted as a tool for overview and coarse connectivity analysis, especially when graph simplification is unavailable or unsuitable.
sections.heading: Limits And Interpretation

source_dossier.summary_long: Ersoy, Hurter, Paulovich, Cantareira, and Telea propose skeleton-based edge bundling for visualizing large general graphs whose node positions are already known. The central idea is to turn groups of geometrically similar edges into thin image-space shapes and then use each shape's medial-axis skeleton as the centerline toward which the edges should be attracted. This reframes bundling as a sequence of edge clustering, distance-transform construction, skeleton extraction, skeleton-path selection, and endpoint-preserving edge advection. The paper's reasoning path is mathematical and procedural: sampled-edge distances create coherent clusters; distance fields inflate cluster drawings into shapes; skeletons identify local centers of those shapes; feature transforms provide attraction directions; and a regularization step prevents singular attraction artifacts from becoming visible kinks. The implementation emphasizes graphics hardware, using CUDA distance and feature transforms, hole filling, skeletonization, path computation, and independent edge attraction to achieve seconds-scale performance on several graph examples. The result is a method that can produce organic, branching bundles or smoother force-directed-like curves depending on smoothing and relaxation choices. Its practical interpretation is deliberately limited: the visual output helps users see coarse routes, topic-to-topic citation structure, air traffic corridors, or migration-like patterns, but it does not preserve individual edge identity or exact direction. The paper is therefore strongest as a layout and interaction technique for structural overview, not as a lossless representation of graph topology.
source_dossier.summary_short: This source introduces skeleton-based edge bundling, which uses medial axes of inflated edge clusters as graph-layout guides. It combines sampled-edge clustering, distance-field skeletons, endpoint-preserving attraction, GPU acceleration, and visual postprocessing to reveal coarse connectivity while obscuring individual edge detail.

sections.body: The survey begins from a concrete systems pressure: VR applications require real-time responses while scenes become more expensive to render. The 13 ms latency tolerance and the observation that delayed content can conflict with user interaction ground the problem in perception rather than only hardware throughput. This makes foveated rendering a practical response to a user-experience constraint.
sections.heading: Performance Motivation

sections.body: The core mechanism is asymmetric human visual sensitivity. The source explains that the fovea supports clear central vision, while peripheral regions can tolerate reduced quality. Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity models turn that biological fact into rendering rules, indicating where spatial, temporal, luminance, or chromatic detail can be reduced with limited perceptual cost.
sections.heading: Perceptual Mechanism

sections.body: The paper does not treat foveated rendering as one technique. It frames the area as a combination of perceptual modeling, multi-quality regional rendering, and integration into renderer architectures. This framing is useful because a method can fail by using the wrong perception model, by choosing poor quality falloff, or by being incompatible with the rendering pipeline it is supposed to accelerate.
sections.heading: Three Design Problems

sections.body: The taxonomy is the survey's organizing contribution. By classifying methods by data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm, it connects design decisions to implementation contexts. The categories also prevent overly narrow comparisons: a technique for mesh rasterization, volume ray casting, hologram phase retrieval, or 360-degree video transmission may all be foveated, but they solve different engineering problems.
sections.heading: Taxonomy Contribution

sections.body: The application of the taxonomy to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021 gives the survey more than a conceptual structure. It functions as a map of the literature, separating early approaches from the more recent decade and showing how methods diversified across data representations, principles, and renderer types as hardware and application needs changed.
sections.heading: Historical Coverage

sections.body: The source is careful about evaluation limits. Existing objective metrics such as FSNR, FWQI, FMSE, and WSSIM each omit or assume important perceptual factors, such as spatio-temporal contrast sensitivity, fixation position, or saliency-model accuracy. That means performance gains alone are not enough; comparability depends on better perceptual metrics and datasets.
sections.heading: Limits and Assumptions

sections.body: For designers, the practical message is that foveated rendering should be chosen and evaluated as a system-level tradeoff among perception, data representation, rendering algorithm, display hardware, and task. The open problems around AR fusion, holograms, light fields, gaze prediction, AI reconstruction, and task guidance suggest that the field remains active even where core VR mesh and volume concepts are mature.
sections.heading: Practical Interpretation

source_dossier.summary_long: The source is a broad survey of foveated rendering, centered on the idea that VR and related interactive graphics systems cannot simply render every part of every scene at maximum quality when scene complexity and human latency tolerance are both severe constraints. The paper motivates the field with the increasing cost of rendering diverse materials, dynamic objects, and complex physical phenomena, and with the approximately 13 ms visual-latency tolerance discussed in its introduction. Against that background, foveated rendering is presented as a perceptual allocation strategy: render the foveal region at high quality, render peripheral regions at lower quality, and rely on human visual-system limits so that the user does not perceive unacceptable loss. The survey's argument is structured around three problems that any foveated method must solve: it must use an appropriate perceptual model, decide how quality varies across regions, and fit that decision into a concrete rendering paradigm. The perceptual discussion emphasizes visual acuity and contrast sensitivity models, including spatial, temporal, luminance, chromatic, and binocular considerations. The taxonomy then turns those concerns into a practical classification with three axes: input data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm. This lets the paper compare work on image/video, volumes, meshes, point clouds, holograms, and light fields, as well as principles such as multi-spatial resolution, multi-temporal resolution, multi-luminance resolution, multi-color resolution, and level of detail. The rendering-paradigm axis includes rasterization, ray tracing, ray casting, instant radiosity, shadow mapping, simplification, neural rendering, photon mapping, phase retrieval, and data transmission. By applying the taxonomy to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021, the survey presents the field as mature in some areas, especially volume data and geometric meshes, but still unresolved in others. Its discussion highlights open problems in broader use of human visual features, AI-assisted gaze and reconstruction methods, emerging data types such as holograms and light fields, objective quality metrics, AR fusion constraints, and task-oriented uses beyond speed improvement alone.
source_dossier.summary_short: This survey presents foveated rendering as a response to the real-time burden of complex VR scenes and the perceptual consequences of latency. It explains how human visual-system models let renderers concentrate fidelity near gaze while reducing work in peripheral regions. Its main contribution is a taxonomy organized by data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm, applied to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021.

source_records.summary: Wang, Shi, and Liu survey foveated rendering as a perceptually grounded acceleration strategy for VR and related display systems. The source frames the field around HVS perceptual models, regional quality variation, and integration into rendering paradigms, then proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy and applies it to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021.

sections.body: The paper's core argument is that large graph drawings can remain interactive if the renderer summarizes both nodes and edges in image space. Rather than drawing every node and edge as a separate mark, it creates node density fields and derives edge aggregates from those fields, giving users an adjustable level-of-detail view that still operates directly on graph data.
sections.heading: Central Argument

sections.body: The node method begins with kernel-density rendering but avoids the cost of placing a kernel texture for every visible node. Its seed-point method first accumulates nodes into pixel-sized bins and then renders weighted kernel rectangles for occupied pixels. This preserves the density field for the viewport while reducing geometry and avoiding stored quadtree-style meta nodes.
sections.heading: Node Aggregation Path

sections.body: Edges are aggregated by using the node accumulation field as a height field. Endpoint pixels climb toward local density maxima, so edges between the same source and target clusters collapse into shared visual aggregates while intra-cluster edges disappear. The result is an implicit edge summary tied closely to the node aggregation rather than a separately precomputed bundle hierarchy.
sections.heading: Edge Aggregation Path

sections.body: The performance case combines an explicit complexity expression with measured GPU timings. The expression bounds rectangle work by min(nodes, pixels) and keeps edge rendering linear in edge count. Table 1 then shows subsecond overview times for several datasets through roughly million-edge scale, with slower but still interactive-ish times for more difficult multi-million-edge or bad-case views.
sections.heading: Performance Evidence

sections.body: The LaGO system turns the rendering technique into an exploration workflow. Zoom and pan change the viewport, the bandwidth parameter supports semantic zoom, normalization and scaling control density-to-color mapping, and click-based detail-on-demand labeling helps identify prominent cluster members. These controls matter because aggregation levels and density ranges vary strongly during exploration.
sections.heading: Interactive Interpretation

sections.body: The examples ground the technique in recognizable graph-analysis tasks. Air-traffic views highlight hubs and the Los Angeles to San Francisco connection; migration views show regional flows such as New York to Florida; Net50 exposes structured cross patterns and central peaks; random data avoids spurious patterns; and the OpenStreetMap example scales to 37.6 million building nodes.
sections.heading: Example Findings

sections.body: The method assumes the graph fits in video memory and that image-space aggregation is an acceptable representation of structure at the current viewport and bandwidth. It can be less advantageous when nearly every node occupies a distinct pixel, and its interpretive examples do not replace formal perceptual validation. The authors themselves identify dynamic kernel-size selection and user study as future work.
sections.heading: Assumptions and Limits

source_dossier.summary_long: This source addresses the practical problem of drawing graphs that fit into video memory but become unreadable as ordinary node-link diagrams because nodes and edges overplot. The authors propose a level-of-detail rendering pipeline that treats node groups as density fields and uses those density fields to guide edge aggregation. The node side adapts kernel-density rendering for graphics hardware, then introduces a seed-point optimization: nodes that land in the same pixel are accumulated first, and only one weighted kernel rectangle is rendered for that pixel. The edge side interprets the node accumulation field as a height field, moves edge endpoints toward local density maxima by hill climbing, and draws implicit aggregate edges between visual clusters. This creates a coupled visual metaphor in which dense node areas and the edges between them change together as the user zooms. The paper's strongest evidence is a combination of formal and empirical support. It gives a cost expression linear in node count, edge count, and the number of seed points bounded by pixels, then reports rendering times for datasets ranging from hundreds of edges to millions of edges and tens of millions of points. The LaGO prototype adds the interaction layer: zooming, panning, bandwidth-linked semantic zoom, normalization controls, color mapping, and detail-on-demand labeling. The examples show why the approach is useful: it exposes flight hubs, migration clusters, Net50 connectivity patterns, random-data non-patterns, and OpenStreetMap building-density structure. The limits are also clear. The method is display- and viewport-dependent, random or evenly distributed nodes can reduce the seed-point advantage, kernel bandwidth choices affect interpretation, and the examples are demonstrations rather than a controlled perceptual evaluation.
source_dossier.summary_short: This source presents an OpenGL level-of-detail renderer for large graph drawings. It combines density-based node aggregation with image-space edge cumulation so users can explore large graphs interactively without precomputed hierarchies. The evidence includes algorithm design, complexity analysis, rendering-time tables, and dataset examples.

sections.body: The sources repeatedly use fields, sampled spaces, or local geometric summaries to decide how visual elements should move, merge, or be rendered. Large-graph level-of-detail rendering treats node density as a height field and hill-climbs edge endpoints toward cluster maxima, while skeleton-based edge bundling constructs distance-field shapes and attracts edges toward skeleton paths.
sections.heading: Field-Guided Aggregation

sections.body: Shadercoding and raymarching provide a related but broader rendering concept: spatial or distance-field descriptions can generate image structure inside fragment shaders. The connection is conceptual rather than identical, because the graph papers use fields for aggregation and layout readability, while shadercoding uses mathematical fields for image synthesis and live visual construction.
sections.heading: Shader And Distance-Field Parallels

sections.body: This topic can synthesize how spatial abstractions turn raw geometry or graph data into controllable visual structure. The evidence supports comparing density fields, feature transforms, skeleton paths, and signed distance fields as field-like mechanisms, while distinguishing their different goals in graph readability and image generation.
sections.heading: Synthesis Boundary

topics.title: Fields and local structure as guides for visual aggregation

sections.body: The sources converge on graphics pipelines where mathematical structure becomes visible through GPU-oriented computation. Shadercoding describes GPU-directed programs that map spatial or pixel data into images through functions, vectors, matrices, and fragment operations. Skeleton-based edge bundling reports CUDA image-space distance transforms, feature transforms, skeletonization, path computation, and attraction as a fast alternative to a CPU AFMM implementation.
sections.heading: Computation as visual pipeline

sections.body: Crowd rendering adds a performance-oriented variant of the same theme: compressed textures, multipass rendering, compact frame storage, and impostor databases make large animated populations render interactively. The shared topic should preserve the different goals of the sources: shadercoding emphasizes expressive image creation, edge bundling emphasizes graph readability, and crowd rendering emphasizes scalable virtual-environment display.
sections.heading: Different real-time goals

topics.title: GPU pipelines turn mathematical structure into real-time images

sections.body: Across the edge-bundling and crowd-rendering sources, dense visual scenes become manageable by replacing raw geometric complexity with structured image-space or sample-based abstractions. Skeleton-based edge bundling clusters geometrically similar edges, inflates cluster shapes, extracts skeletons, and attracts edges toward locally centered targets; image-based crowd rendering uses impostor samples, positional and directional discretization, and optimized texture storage to display large animated crowds at interactive rates.
sections.heading: Shared abstraction strategy

sections.body: The shared concept is not merely acceleration: abstraction changes what the viewer can read. Edge bundling sacrifices individual edge identity and direction fidelity to expose coarse connectivity, while crowd impostors trade full per-avatar geometry for scalable visual presence. Shader raymarching provides a related but weaker bridge because it also treats geometry through mathematical spatial descriptions, marching rays through distance fields inside a fragment shader.
sections.heading: Readable but partial representations

topics.title: Image-space geometric abstraction for readable visual complexity

sections.body: Several sources describe real-time graphics pipelines that trade exact per-element rendering for perceptually or analytically useful aggregation. In large graph rendering, density-based node aggregation, edge cumulation, pixel-bin seed points, and a two-pass accumulation field reduce work while preserving the density field for a viewport. Image-based crowd rendering similarly uses impostors, compressed textures, compact frame storage, and directional or positional discretization to keep dense animated crowds interactive.
sections.heading: Shared Pattern

sections.body: The shared concept is not a single algorithm but a design pattern: move expensive visual structure into screen-space, image-space, or precomputed image representations that fit GPU rendering workflows. This pattern appears in OpenGL graph level-of-detail rendering, image-based crowd impostors, CUDA-assisted edge bundling, and foveated rendering's regional quality allocation.
sections.heading: GPU And Image-Space Execution

sections.body: The evidence supports a topic focused on scale management, with caveats that each source optimizes a different visual object: graph nodes and edges, animated crowds, bundled connectivity, or perceptual display regions. The common synthesis is therefore about practical real-time rendering strategies rather than a single interchangeable technique.
sections.heading: Scope And Caveats

topics.title: Image-space GPU aggregation for real-time visual scale

sections.body: Large visual datasets are made useful by combining overview summaries with interaction mechanisms that let users recover selected detail. LaGO supports zooming, panning, normalization controls, color mapping, and detail-on-demand labels, and its examples show recognizable patterns in flights, migration, Net50, and OpenStreetMap data.
sections.heading: Overview Before Detail

sections.body: This connects to skeleton-based edge bundling's coarse-scale connectivity focus and to foveated rendering's principle of allocating quality unevenly according to perceptual need. In each case, the visualization is intentionally not uniform: it emphasizes structures likely to matter while accepting some loss, reduction, or quality variation elsewhere.
sections.heading: Selective Fidelity

sections.body: The topic should frame these systems as interactive summary interfaces, not as lossless data displays. The evidence explicitly warns that bundling can obscure individual edges and distort directions, and foveation similarly depends on perceptual assumptions that guide where quality can safely be reduced.
sections.heading: Interpretation Limits

topics.title: Interactive visual summaries and detail on demand

sections.body: Foveated rendering and image-based impostor rendering both respond to real-time rendering pressure by reducing work where full geometric or full-quality rendering is not necessary. Foveated rendering allocates high quality to the foveal region and lower quality to peripheral regions, while crowd impostors replace complex human models with optimized image samples to keep dense virtual environments interactive.
sections.heading: Section 1

sections.body: The shared concept is selective fidelity: rendering systems can preserve the experience that matters to the viewer while changing the underlying representation, quality, or detail level. The foveated-rendering survey frames this around human-visual-system models and regional quality variation; the crowd-rendering system frames it around positional and directional discretization, texture compression, and impostors.
sections.heading: Section 2

sections.body: This topic should also note the limits of the comparison. Foveated rendering is explicitly perceptual and spans many rendering paradigms, whereas the crowd-rendering source focuses on a concrete image-based technique for animated humans in virtual cities. Both nevertheless treat rendering cost as a central design constraint for interactive visual systems.
sections.heading: Section 3

topics.title: Perceptual and image-based strategies for real-time rendering acceleration

sections.body: Foveated rendering, edge bundling, and image-based crowd rendering all make controlled tradeoffs between visual utility and complete information. Foveated rendering intentionally lowers peripheral quality to preserve perceived quality; edge bundling reveals coarse connectivity while overdraw and distorted directions obscure individual edges; crowd impostors reduce geometric complexity and texture memory while introducing concerns such as viewpoint-change popping.
sections.heading: Section 1

sections.body: The shared concept is not simply optimization, but acceptable loss. These systems identify what must remain legible or perceptually convincing, then choose where detail can be compressed, approximated, merged, or regionally reduced. The evidence suggests that graphics methods often succeed by matching loss to the task: comfort and perceived quality in VR, coarse connectivity in graphs, and dense animated presence in virtual cities.
sections.heading: Section 2

sections.body: A balanced treatment should preserve the caveat that each source names different risks. Foveated rendering is concerned with latency, HVS modeling, and integration into rendering paradigms; edge bundling warns about destroyed edge-level information; crowd rendering addresses popping, texture memory, avatar variety, and shadow consistency.
sections.heading: Section 3

topics.title: Quality tradeoffs and information loss in visual systems

sections.body: Both sources treat real-time rendering as more than offline image production: shadercoding becomes a timed public or improvisational performance, while image-based crowd rendering is judged by whether dense animated scenes remain interactive.
sections.heading: Shared Live Constraint

sections.body: The shared concept is performance under live constraints. The shadercoding source emphasizes code, image, performer, and audience; the crowd-rendering source emphasizes frame-rate evidence for thousands of moving humans in a virtual city.
sections.heading: Performance Evidence

sections.body: A topic page should keep the domains distinct: one source concerns artistic live coding, while the other concerns rendering-system engineering, but both rely on technical control to sustain real-time visual experience.
sections.heading: Domain Boundary

topics.title: Real-time graphics as a performance medium

sections.body: The sources share a concern with replacing full physical or geometric complexity with computable spatial abstractions that can still produce convincing images in real time.
sections.heading: Abstracted Space

sections.body: In shadercoding, fragment shaders map pixel positions to colors and raymarching reconstructs depth by stepping through distance fields. In crowd rendering, impostors, directional discretization, PCA-adjusted planes, tile grids, and projected shadows approximate people, motion constraints, and lighting cues.
sections.heading: Rendering Techniques

sections.body: The synthesis is strongest at the level of technique rather than purpose: one source uses mathematical fields and pixels for digital-art imagery, while the other uses image samples and spatial discretization for scalable animated crowds.
sections.heading: Synthesis Limit

sections.body: Several sources describe graphics methods that introduce an intermediate spatial guide to decide where computation, quality, or motion should go. Foveated rendering uses gaze-centered perceptual regions to guide quality allocation; image-based crowd rendering subdivides the environment into tiles for collision and shadowing; skeleton-based edge bundling extracts skeleton paths from inflated edge-cluster shapes to guide bundled edge geometry.
sections.heading: Section 1

sections.body: These guides differ in form but share a role: they simplify decisions across a complex visual system. Perceptual regions encode viewer sensitivity, tiles encode local environment behavior, and skeletons encode locally centered bundle targets. In each case, a spatial abstraction mediates between raw scene or data complexity and a tractable rendering or visualization operation.
sections.heading: Section 2

sections.body: The evidence supports a synthesis around control structures rather than a single algorithmic family. The methods are not interchangeable: foveated rendering is a perceptual rendering strategy, crowd tiles support simulation-adjacent rendering decisions, and graph skeletons support visualization layout. The common theme is that spatial structure can organize where visual fidelity, interaction constraints, or geometric attraction should be applied.
sections.heading: Section 3

topics.title: Spatial guides as compact control structures in graphics computation

sections.body: The foveated-rendering survey explicitly organizes a broad field by required input data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm, applying that taxonomy to 90 reports. That classification can be synthesized with the other sources as a broader need in graphics: complex techniques become easier to compare when described by their inputs, representational abstractions, computational principles, and visual outputs.
sections.heading: Section 1

sections.body: Shadercoding, crowd impostors, and skeleton-based edge bundling each emphasize a different abstraction boundary. Shadercoding describes GPU programs that transform spatial data and physical properties into images, including fragment shaders and raymarching distance fields. Crowd rendering uses image databases, impostor planes, alpha-guided passes, and compressed textures. Edge bundling uses sampled edges, clustering, distance-field shapes, skeletons, and GPU image-space transforms.
sections.heading: Section 2

sections.body: A useful page would not claim that these sources share the same taxonomy. Instead, it would use the foveated-rendering taxonomy as a seed for a concept page about how graphics literature classifies methods across input representation, rendering paradigm, performance goal, and perceptual or visual tradeoff.
sections.heading: Section 3

topics.title: Taxonomies and abstractions for comparing rendering paradigms

sections.body: The graphics sources repeatedly present constraints as productive rather than merely limiting. Shadercoding turns mathematical and GPU-programming constraints into a live digital-art practice; foveated rendering uses limits of real-time VR hardware and human perception to guide new rendering strategies; edge bundling accepts information loss to reveal coarse connectivity; crowd rendering uses impostor and texture constraints to enable dense virtual cities.
sections.heading: Section 1

sections.body: This topic can connect artistic and engineering accounts of constraint. In shadercoding, technical mastery supports improvisation and expressive performance. In foveated rendering and crowd rendering, perceptual, memory, and latency constraints motivate selective rendering. In edge bundling, the limitation that individual edges become less separable is reframed around the exploratory value of coarse-scale patterns.
sections.heading: Section 2

sections.body: The synthesis should avoid flattening artistic and technical aims into one motivation. The evidence supports a broader concept: graphics practice often turns limits in computation, perception, representation, or interface into design rules that shape what visual experiences become possible.
sections.heading: Section 3

topics.title: Technical constraints as generative conditions for graphics practice

sections.body: Both sources frame technical limits as productive rather than merely restrictive. Shadercoding treats mathematical and programming constraints as conditions for artistic creation; crowd rendering turns memory, texture, and model-complexity limits into concrete rendering strategies.
sections.heading: Constraints As Productive Conditions

sections.body: The crowd-rendering evidence is operational: sample packing, OpenGL texture compression, compact animation-frame storage, and alpha-channel multipass recoloring reduce memory pressure while preserving or expanding visual variety.
sections.heading: Crowd Rendering Optimizations

sections.body: The shadercoding evidence is conceptual and practice-oriented: mathematical fluency enables original shaders, and mastered technical constraints can become creative motors for digital art. A topic should avoid claiming the crowd-rendering paper makes an artistic argument, but can compare how constraints shape image-making in both cases.
sections.heading: Artistic Comparison Boundary

sections.body: A cross-source page can synthesize how computed graphics systems expose controls that improve visual legibility or variety while accepting artifacts, constraints, or information loss. Skeleton-based edge bundling lets users tune smoothing, relaxation, and cushion shading, but the same method is limited because bundling overdraws individual edges and distorts directions. Crowd rendering similarly uses PCA-informed impostor planes to reduce popping, alpha-channel multipass recoloring to add variation, and shadow projection to preserve posture cues, all within an impostor-based approximation.
sections.heading: Controls and approximations

sections.body: Shadercoding supplies a conceptual parallel: mathematical and technical constraints can become creative motors, and mastery of the code-image system can support live improvisation. The evidence is stronger for technical tradeoffs in edge bundling and crowd rendering than for direct equivalence with performance art, so this topic frames shadercoding as an interpretive extension rather than the core evidence.
sections.heading: Creative extension

topics.title: Visual control tradeoffs in computed graphics
